working_title: Handwired: How an Ordinary Program Becomes an Exact Neural Net (and Learns Anyway)
audience: Curious general viewers (teenagers through adults) with no assumed math or CS background, plus working programmers and ML practitioners who want the real mechanics; every number and construction on screen must survive a practitioner checking it by hand or by running the code at chenglou/handwired@257856e.
central_questions: What is a Handwired program: which primitives (FP32 weighted sums, gated relu / reglu, boolean and indexRead operations) does it reduce JavaScript to, and how are cells, wires, the source table and builder code appending to a Circuit organized?
How exactly does the README example (a > 4) ? 10 : 12 become relu arithmetic, with real numbers on screen, and why do both branches always run while a 0/1 selector picks one?

What does 'exact' mean in FP32 here: which declared ranges, rounding points, comparison rules (emitCompare) and magnitude limits make the arithmetic agree with JavaScript, and where are the limits (non-integers, dynamic division)?
How is a whole program compiled into one big matmul (layers, fusion, sparsity) and run on the JS CPU evaluator or WebGPU, and what do the measured costs look like?

How do loops and state become fixed-size arithmetic: the host loop (inputs in, evaluate, next state copied back, DOM writes), why a program cannot stop early, and the patterns (counts, trees, tables, prefix networks, sort, filter+slice into K nodes, same work on every item)?
How are springs and time handled inside a program with no clock of its own?
What do the three demos (HandwiredOS, the learned gallery, JSON search over 100,000 documents per keystroke) actually do and measure?
What does differentiability buy: how do gradients flow through a handwritten program, what happens when weights are unfrozen and trained end to end, and what did the lab find learns or does not?
Where does this sit relative to the old idea that neurons compute logic (McCulloch and Pitts, 1943) and modern work compiling programs into networks, and what is still open as of 2026-10-27?

topics.title: Framing: From Logical Neurons to Programs Compiled into Networks
questions: What exactly did McCulloch and Pitts (1943) claim a net of idealized threshold neurons could compute, in their own words, and how was that claim received and later qualified?
What did Kleene (1951/1956) and later Siegelmann and Sontag (1992/1995) show about what neural nets can compute, and with which caveats (rational weights, unbounded precision)?

What do modern 'compile a program into a network' efforts claim: RASP (Weiss, Goldberg, Yahav 2021), Tracr (Lindner et al. 2023), looped transformers as programmable computers (Giannou et al. 2023)? How do they differ from Handwired (transformer weights vs. matmul + relu/reglu for UI programs)?

Does the Handwired repo itself cite or position itself against any of this prior work (search README, docs, lab/research-sweep.md)? If not, the film must present the framing as context, not as the author's lineage.
What is the belief of the age today about hand-written vs. learned weights, and who argues for/against compiled networks (e.g., mechanistic interpretability uses of Tracr)?
must_cover: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts, 'A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity' (Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics, 1943) — verbatim key sentence only if verified
Stephen Kleene, 'Representation of Events in Nerve Nets and Finite Automata' (RAND 1951 / Automata Studies 1956)
Hava Siegelmann and Eduardo Sontag on Turing-complete recurrent nets (1992/1995) and the precision caveat
RASP: Gail Weiss, Yoav Goldberg, Eran Yahav, 'Thinking Like Transformers' (ICML 2021)
Tracr: David Lindner et al., DeepMind, 2023
Giannou et al., 'Looped Transformers as Programmable Computers' (ICML 2023)
Whether chenglou/handwired references any of these (lab/research-sweep.md); keep framing brief and labeled as context
Contested: whether 'neurons compute logic' was ever biologically right (later neuroscience dissent)
